newsitem.title: CHINA: RTRS-ASIAN SUGAR - Far East trade quiet, awaits China.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-ASIAN SUGAR - Far East trade quiet, awaits China.

text.p: While Far East sugar traders said on Wednesday they were waiting for China's sugar imports to begin, Chinese producers worried the domestic market could be swamped and already-low prices pushed further down.
White sugar prices in China's southern production belt are still below 4,000 yuan ($481) per tonne, in some places dipping to 3,700 yuan ($445), traders and industry sources there said.
Break-even point was above 4,000 yuan per tonne, and ideally should be up to 4,200 to 4,300 yuan per tonne for the factories to make any money at all, a senior industry executive said.
"We don't expect buying orders from China at least until the second half of this year. Thai premiums are likely to ease further in the near term," a sugar trader at a Tokyo trade house said.
Japanese traders are watching whether the sugar buying orders issued by Chinese authorities will prop up domestic sugar prices.

The official China Daily said last week the Ministry of Internal Trade had issued an urgent circular to government sugar firms nationwide to buy sugar to boost reserves, support output and stabilise the market.
"Depressed local prices were behind China's reluctance to re-enter the market. We'd like to see how the action changes the prices," another sugar trader said.
Official Chinese media said China planned to import 690,000 tonnes of sugar in 1997.
Of that amount, 350,000 tonnes would come from Cuba, where, according to German statistician F.O. Licht, the 1996/97 sugar crop should be close to the forecast of 4.5 million tonnes.
The remainder of China's 1997 imports would come from Thailand and Australia, traders said.
Official customs figures show total 1996 sugar imports were 1.25 million tonnes, 57.5 percent down on the previous year.
One Hong Kong-based sugar trader said China's 1997 sugar imports would probably be closer to 1.5 million tonnes.

A Hong Kong-based executive responsible for several sugar facilities in southern China, however, said that unless the Chinese government controlled the way in which the imported sugar reached the market, prices could be expected to fall.
"If it is tightly controlled and it trickles onto the market, it would be okay," he said.

China's official 1996/97 sugar production target has varied over the past few months, in one case going over eight million tonnes. Traders in the region have tended to put more store in an earlier figure of 6.53 million tonnes.
China's annual demand is around eight million tonnes.
Japanese traders said Thai raw premiums have been easing since earlier this week, reflecting the lack of Chinese buying.
Traders said premiums for March/May delivery were quoted at 0.30/0.40 cents (bid/offer) per pound over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on an FOB (free on board) basis.
May/July deliveries were quoted at 0.40/0.45 cents on the New York exchange, and July/September at 0.75/0.85 cents, they said.
Mitsubishi Corp last week confirmed it was the supplier of 12,500 tonnes of white sugar to Iraq for January shipment under an oil-for-food deal reached with the United Nations.
Mitsubishi said further sugar sales depended on the Iraqis. No further deals by the trade house could be confirmed.
-- Eiichiro Tokumoto, Tokyo commodities desk 81-3-3432-7391
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai newsroom 86-21-6279-7004
